thread.title: Berkshire Hathaway's Results Show the Profit Power of Warren Buffett's Conglomerate

title: Berkshire Hathaway's Results Show the Profit Power of Warren Buffett's Conglomerate
text:
Berkshire Hathaway’s Results Show the Profit Power of Warren Buffett’s Conglomerate By Nov. 5, 2018 11:41 a.m. ET Order Reprints Warren Buffett, chairman and chief executive of Berkshire Hathaway. Photograph by Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg Text size
Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway made waves this weekend when it disclosed a buyback of nearly $1 billion of its stock, its first buyback since 2012. But what investors are focusing on Monday – and what should encourage them in the months to come – is how powerful a profit machine the conglomerate is.
For the third quarter, operating profits doubled to $6.9 billion. The company also had a 5% gain in its book value per share in the period.
Barclays analyst Jay Gelb lauded the “strong results” in an analyst note on Monday as he lifted his earnings estimates and price targets. Berkshire’s class A shares (ticker: BRK.A) are trading sharply higher this morning, gaining 4.4%, to $322,070, while the company’s class B shares (BRK.B) are up 4.3%, to $215.54.
Gelb lifted his 2018 and 2019 operating profit estimate to $15,186 and $15,524 from $14,494 and $14,766, respectively, and increased his price target on the class A shares by 5%, to $397,500 from $378,000. His class B target goes to $265 from $252 a share.
Berkshire’s total earnings in the quarter of $18.5 billion were a near-record for any company – trailing only Apple’s $20.1 billion in the quarter ended Dec. 31, 2017. The huge earnings reflected paper profits on Berkshire’s $218 billion equity portfolio that must be reflected in quarterly results under accounting rules that took effect this year. Barron’s wrote last week that the total profits could be a near record for any company. And we have been bullish on Berkshire shares.
The operating earnings rose to $4,197 per class A share from $2,093, a 100% increase. The profits exceeded the consensus estimate of $3,827 a share by about 10%.
CEO Buffett urges investors to focus on the operating earnings excluding the realized and unrealized investment gains. Those results were stellar as Berkshire’s insurance operations benefited from a relatively mild hurricane activity in the period relative to a year ago, when three major storms, including Harvey, hit. Insurance operations swung to a $2.1 billion profit from a loss of nearly $1 billion a year ago and the Burlington Northern railroad showed a 10% gain in operating profit, to $1.9 billion.
Berkshire is benefiting from the strength in the U.S. economy given the domestic focus on most of its businesses as well as the lower corporate tax rate.
“The business is performing well,” says Trip Miller, a managing partner at Gullane Capital Partners in Memphis, a longtime Berkshire holder. “Buffett has built an earnings machine that is recession resistant,” Read More Preparing Berkshire for a Future Without Buffett
Investors were eager to see the extent of Berkshire’s buybacks as an indication about Buffett’s views on the appeal of the stock . The company repurchased $928 million in the period, above Gelb’s $500 million estimate. The estimates amounted to guesswork because Berkshire hadn’t repurchased any stock since 2012. Gelb sees $1.5 billion of repurchases in the fourth quarter and $4 billion in 2019.
While better than nothing in the eyes of Berkshire fans, the buybacks are running at annual rate of less than 1% of Berkshire’s shares outstanding – way below the 5%-plus buybacks executed by many big financial companies. Buffett has long been cool to buybacks at Berkshire while advocating them at many of the companies where Berkshire is invested.
Berkshire pays no dividend and probably won’t do so as long as the 88-year-old Buffett is at the helm.
The buybacks are modest relative to Berkshire’s huge cash pile that totals about $103 billion. Berkshire continues to be very quiet on the acquisition front as Buffett appears to struggle in finding attractively priced businesses at a time when private equity and corporations are flush with cash.
Berkshire’s book value was up 5% in the quarter, to $228,712 per class A share and the stock now trades at 1.4 times book, an appealing level according to bulls like Gelb. Book could be pressured somewhat in the current quarter by the weakness in the stock market and Berkshire’s largest equity holding, Apple (AAPL).
Gelb wrote Monday that Berkshire “looks well-positioned to benefit from an expanding economy, higher short-term rates, and potential future accretive acquisitions.” He sees solid growth of 10% in book value in 2019.
